It has, however, come at a cost. Several influential politicians were forced to shelve their ambitions and make way for incumbent governors, some of whom Nentawe and President Bola Tinubu have only just welcomed into the party.
Virtually all the state governors seeking re-election were handed the party’s tickets unopposed. The exception was Siminalayi Fubara of Rivers State, who was denied the ticket, also unopposed.
So, it is a surprise that there aren’t more court cases challenging the outcome of party primaries across the states. The party initially withheld the names on the final list of candidates.
And when INEC published the final list, there was still no uproar or flood of court cases. Nentawe deserves credit for this. It appears many had been compensated in cash and in kind.
Still, the APC is walking into the elections with open wounds in states crucial to its victory, as old rivalries are resurfacing and political alliances are crumbling. Influential party figures are drawing battle lines in what appears to be an increasingly fierce struggle for political relevance and control.
What is happening in Kano, Benue, Katsina and Nasarawa is more than a collection of isolated disagreements.
In Kano, the cracks have become difficult to conceal. APC chieftain Aminu Shehu Sharada has openly acknowledged that all is not well within the party, appealing to President Tinubu and Abdulaziz Yari to intervene.
His warning that those portraying the state chapter as united are not giving the President an accurate picture underscores the seriousness of the divisions.
In Benue, the longstanding disagreement between Governor Hyacinth Alia and the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), George Akume, continues to threaten party cohesion.
Their competing political structures and disagreements over the governor’s second-term ambition have exposed a struggle for supremacy. The recent court victory by former governor Gabriel Suswam, affirming his victory in the senatorial primary, adds another dimension to the complicated political calculations in the state.
Katsina presents another revealing picture. Presidential aide Ibrahim Masari has publicly discussed his differences with Governor Dikko Radda, bringing a hostile relationship into the open.
In Nasarawa, the relationship between Tanko Al-Makura and his successor, Governor Abdullahi Sule, has also deteriorated. Their disagreement, particularly Sule’s preference for Aliyu Wadada and Al-Makura’s support for former IGP Mohammed Adamu, has effectively created opposing political camps.
If left unattended, these wounds could spread across key organs of the APC. That means other contests and other states. Kano, Katsina and perhaps two more states in the North-West could slip away from the APC at the presidential election.
The same could happen in the North-Central, leaving Yilwatda Nentawe scratching his head .
